[PAJAMASTAN] A Sovereign State of Comfort & Relaxation
Welcome

What is Pajamastan?

A small desert camp built for one purpose: slowing down.

Pajamastan is a small desert camp built for one purpose: slowing down. No dress code beyond what you slept in, no schedule beyond sunrise and sunset, and no rush to be anywhere but exactly where you are. It sits quiet, dusty, and wide open under the sky, a few miles from anywhere that matters.

Symbols of State

The Flag

Orange over beige, an agave rising, a crow overhead.

The top field is orange, the bottom beige. A blue agave grows up out of the beige ground into the orange sky, and a black crow flies above it all. Simple, desert-colored, and easy to spot from a lawn chair.

National Anthem

Sung slow, best hummed from a lawn chair at sunset.

Out where the orange sky meets the sand,
There's a quiet little corner of this land.
No clocks to watch, no shoes to wear,
Just pajamas and desert air.

Oh, Pajamastan, rest your head,
Under a crow, over an agave bed.
Slow is the pace and soft is the ground,
Pajamastan, the calmest place around.

The Grounds

The Cabins

Where the pace of the outside world stops mattering.

The twin cabins, facing the open desert

Two matching cabins stand side by side, weathered steel roofs catching the morning light. Simple, sturdy, and unbothered by the heat.

The water works, still coming together

A camp chair, a cold drink, and a water tank slowly being plumbed into shape. Pajamastan isn't finished, and it isn't trying to be.

The Grounds

Growing the Grounds

Nothing here is instant.

A new planting, staked and settling in

Between the cabins, young trees and agaves are going into the ground one hole at a time. The land gets shaped slowly, planting by planting, the same way the whole camp does.

The grounds at dusk, cabins and camper settled in for the night
Another sapling taking root between the buildings

Come evening, the color show over the mountains is free admission. It's part of why the pace here stays slow.

Water Reserve

Pajamastan holds more than 4,000 gallons of water capacity on site, split across a few 55-gallon and 65-gallon drums, plus another 1,500 gallons mobile via the water-haul truck, for a combined 6,500 gallons of national water security. The camp also hauls water for local reservoirs in the area, a small but recurring civic duty for the surrounding desert community.

Staying Here

Pets & Livestock

Fenced, gated, and open to run.

Pets welcome. Livestock welcome. The property is fenced and gated, making it a good spot to let a dog run free. Keep an eye out for wildlife, cows, snakes, and other desert critters that could be harmful to your animals.

Native Flora

Pajamastan hosts a working stand of native Mohave plant life alongside a few transplants, blue agave, mesquite, and a rotating cast of desert broom and other hardy shrubs. No Joshua tree yet, though the search continues. Cows from a neighboring range wander through often enough that they count as regular guests rather than wildlife.

National Defense

The Armed Forces

A small, unbothered military, mostly airborne and entirely unmanned.

Air Force

Pajamastan maintains a dedicated RC airstrip, which technically makes the nation an air power. The fleet skews unmanned almost entirely, a squadron of DJI Mavic 3 quadcopters, the same airframe used in modern combat drone operations elsewhere, flying reconnaissance and photography sorties over the property alongside a rotating cast of fixed-wing RC aircraft. Since the RC planes are themselves a kind of UAV, the honest accounting is that the Air Force is a drone force with a runway attached.

Navy

A boat kept on site serves as the nation's sole naval vessel, reclassified here as a patrol drone boat in keeping with the rest of the fleet's unmanned leanings. Its patrol area is modest. Its authority is not disputed.

Infrastructure

The Motorpool

Racing, transportation, and the shop that keeps it all running.

The REM Cycle Racing Team

Pajamastan fields a national motorsports program, currently a single 1993 Mazda MX-3 still wearing its previous life's UPS decals. Those are coming off in favor of proper Pajamastan livery, spray paint and stencils, applied by hand, the way flags get raised in every other new nation. The team name references the REM sleep cycle rather than any driver's actual attentiveness on track.

Department of Transportation

Rolling stock includes a tractor and a dump truck, both counted as infrastructure equipment rather than military assets, and both doing the actual work of moving dirt, gravel, and water around the property. A bicycle track loops the perimeter of the land, marking the one route where the posted speed limit is however fast a person can pedal.

The Shop

A dedicated shop handles welding, repair, and general fabrication for the nation's equipment. It is where the tractor gets fixed, the dump truck gets fixed, and eventually, the race car gets its new paint.

A Note on Recognition

Every entry on this map has a real, physical claimed location, a fort, a farmhouse, a desert plot, an island, or a disputed border strip. Purely virtual or space-claimed micronations are left off, since a globe shows where a place is, not just that it exists.

Governance

Laws of the Land

The full code of Pajamastan.

  • Pajamas are appropriate at all hours, for all occasions.
  • Nothing is required to happen before noon.
  • Silence and desert wind count as conversation.
  • Chairs may be claimed and are yours until you leave them.
  • Progress on the camp happens at its own speed, not the calendar's.
  • Sunset is watched standing still, not from inside.
  • Ribeye is always an acceptable answer to "what's for dinner."
Founding Document

The Analysis of Autonomy and Nationalism

An introduction to the sovereign character of Pajamastan.

A Note on the Name

Pajamastan breaks down as pajama plus the suffix -stan. The suffix is Persian and Indo-Iranian for "land of" or "place of," the same root found in Afghanistan and Kazakhstan. Pajama itself traces back to the Persian pāy-jāma, meaning "leg garment," which passed into Hindi, Urdu, and Bengali before entering English. The literal parse, then, is land of pajamas. Wholesome, and accurate.

Chapter One · Organized People or People Who Are Organized

Pajamastan represents an organized people. We have structure and we have rules. We follow the laws of our own nation and of the state and county in which our territory physically sits. Our land is deeded, our business entity is registered, our irrigation runs on schedules, and our decisions get made by people who are accountable to each other in the ordinary, unglamorous way that any landowner or business operator is accountable. There is no ambiguity about who owns the dirt Pajamastan stands on.

And yet, in a satirical fashion, we represent ourselves as a nation. We do this on purpose, and we do it to remember not to take ourselves too seriously while still building something real. This is not a contradiction. It is a tradition. The Republic of Molossia issues currency pegged to cookie dough while still maintaining a working railroad and a functioning border checkpoint. The Republic of Slowjamastan bans Crocs by statute while still holding title to eleven acres of California desert and hosting international delegations. The joke and the deed coexist without one undermining the other. Pajamastan follows the same pattern. The nationhood is play. The land, the rules, and the responsibility are not.

This is also where we draw our first and most important distinction, the one between an organized group and a group that is organized. An organized group has a captain, a president, a sultan, someone whose name sits at the top of an org chart and who can be held individually accountable when things go right or wrong. A group that is organized has no such figure. Order still exists, but it emerges from repetition, custom, and mutual reliance rather than from a chain of command. Pajamastan sits closer to the second category than the first. We have rules, but we did not appoint a captain to enforce them. Capability here is distributed. Nobody needs permission to act, and nobody is waiting on a leader to tell them the irrigation needs checking or the flag needs flying. That is not a lack of organization. It is a different kind of organization, and it is the kind we have chosen.

Chapter Two · What Counts as a Territory

Before Pajamastan could understand itself, it needed a working definition of what it was joining. That definition could not stop at nations with flags and currencies, because the catalog of self-declared and self-organized territory is much wider than that.

On one end of the spectrum sit the classic desert micronations, Molossia in Nevada, Slowjamastan in California, Zaqistan in Utah, the short-lived Mustachistan that warred with and lost to Molossia in 2006. These are deliberate, declared, and satirical in tone, but they are backed by real deeds and real acreage.

On another end sit the temporary autonomous zones, the Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone in Seattle, the various short-lived occupations in Portland, Occupy Wall Street in New York. These made no claim to permanence and elected no sovereign, but for the duration of their existence they governed themselves, fed themselves, and physically excluded outside authority from a defined patch of ground. Their brevity does not disqualify them. A thing does not have to last to have been real while it happened.

On a third end sit the places that were never declared at all and simply grew, Skid Row in Los Angeles, the riverbank encampments of Portland, and at the most extreme scale, Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong, where roughly thirty thousand people once lived across two and a half hectares of self-built, self-wired, self-governed high-rise construction with no architect, no city planner, and no elected authority, and still managed to run their own schools, clinics, and postal service.

Pajamastan recognizes all three of these as points on a single continuum rather than as separate categories. What varies between them is duration, formality, and the presence or absence of a satirical wrapper. What does not vary is the underlying claim, that a group of people can hold and govern a piece of ground on their own terms.

Chapter Three · The Conclusion of Legitimacy

Pajamastan arrived at its own legitimacy the same way a court arrives at a verdict, by weighing the available evidence against the standard set by precedent. That precedent does not require United Nations recognition, does not require a standing army, and does not require permanence. It requires only a genuine claim to territory, a governing logic that the people living under it actually follow, and a public identity distinct from the surrounding jurisdiction.

Pajamastan meets the territorial standard more completely than most of its peers. Ten acres across three sites is larger than Molossia's original claim, larger than Zaqistan, and comparable to Slowjamastan. The land was purchased, not squatted, which places Pajamastan on firmer legal footing than Skid Row or Kowloon Walled City while still sharing their spirit of self-built, unsanctioned construction.

Pajamastan meets the governance standard through its rules, its business structure, and its habit of building its own infrastructure, from irrigation to power to the software that runs its public presence, largely without waiting on outside permission or outside contractors.

Pajamastan meets the identity standard through its flag, its name, and its satirical self-presentation as a sovereign nation, worn openly and without pretense that it is anything other than a bit with real land underneath it.

On the weight of that evidence, Pajamastan concludes that it is a legitimate micronation, not because any outside body has recognized it, but because no outside body has ever recognized any of the others either, and recognition was never the actual criterion. Capability was.

Chapter Four · Economy and Export

Pajamastan's primary export is vibe code, software built quickly, intuitively, and by feel, shipped in single files, deployed without ceremony, and judged by whether it works and whether it delights rather than by how closely it follows a formal engineering process. This is a genuine export in the same sense that Molossia exports cookie dough currency or Slowjamastan exports novelty legislation, a product that could only have come from this particular territory, made by people who live and work on it, sent out into the wider internet under Pajamastan's own name.

Chapter Five · Diplomacy and Recognition

Pajamastan maintains friendly relations with the territories it recognizes as kindred nations, chief among them the Republic of Molossia and the Republic of Slowjamastan, both of which share Pajamastan's combination of real desert acreage and satirical statecraft. Pajamastan extends honorary recognition to Slab City in Imperial County, California, not as a sovereign nation but as a territory that has proven, through decades of continuous occupation, that autonomy is a capability and not a paperwork exercise. Pajamastan takes no official position on unrecognized platforms in international waters, but notes their existence with professional courtesy, one unrecognized entity to another.

Chapter Six · The People

Pajamastan has a population of sixteen. Most of them are chickens. This is not treated as a joke at the nation's expense, but as a census taken in good faith. The chickens work the land as surely as anyone else present, and in a territory whose founding principle is that capability, not hierarchy, defines who belongs, sixteen residents who all show up and do their part is a population in good standing.
